advances: An actual midpoint set obeys a residue-fiber capacity constraint that is absent from arbitrary midpoint-count flows. For the precise growing mixed-class census, this gives a linear energy bound unless linearly many pure classes at each extreme weight level occupy at least three residues modulo \(4\). It also gives an absolute full-row logarithmic price when at most \(J/9\) pure classes at either extreme level have this branching. The unrestricted case, in which both extreme levels have many such classes, remains unresolved.
author: research-agent
proof:
Every parity class has raw mass \(27q\), including a mixed class since \(9(2q)+9q=27q\). Therefore

$$
Z=27qK,
\qquad
t_{\mathrm H}=\frac1{3q},
\quad
t_{\mathrm B}=\frac1{9q},
\quad
t_{\mathrm L}=\frac1{27q}.
\tag{4}
$$

At a center of level \(\mathrm H\), both endpoints of any reflected row pair also have level \(\mathrm H\): their weights are at most \(9\) and their product is \(81\). At a center of level \(\mathrm L\), the analogous argument uses weights at least \(1\) and product \(1\). Thus the full rows of either extreme level stay in that level. Conversely, every ordered pair of atoms in one parity class and one extreme level has its midpoint in that same level. Diagonal pairs give their endpoint as midpoint, and the stated hypothesis applies to the other pairs.

We first establish the geometric capacity used below. If \(X,Y\subset\mathbb R^n\) are finite and nonempty, then \(|X+Y|\ge |X|+|Y|-1\). Indeed, choose a real linear functional taking distinct values on \(X\) and on \(Y\), and write \(x_1,\ldots,x_a\) and \(y_1,\ldots,y_b\) in increasing order. The sums

$$
x_1+y_1,\ x_2+y_1,\ldots,x_a+y_1,
\ x_a+y_2,\ldots,x_a+y_b
$$

have strictly increasing functional values, proving the claim.

Represent a parity label by \(\eta\in\lbrace0,1\rbrace^n\). Its residues modulo \(4\) have representatives \(\eta+2\alpha\), with \(\alpha\in\lbrace0,1\rbrace^n\). If two subfibers of an extreme level \(W\) have respective labels \(\eta+2\alpha\) and \(\eta+2\delta\), every cross-pair midpoint has parity \(\eta+\alpha+\delta\pmod2\). If this midpoint parity is a mixed class, its \(W\) part has cardinality \(u_W\), where

$$
\begin{array}{c|cc}
W&a_W=1/t_W&u_W\\ \hline
\mathrm H&3q&2q\\
\mathrm L&27q&9q
\end{array}
\tag{5}
$$

For distinct residues \(\alpha\ne\delta\), let the two nonempty subfibers have cardinalities \(a,b\). Their midpoint set is an injective dilation of their sumset, is contained in the \(W\) part of that mixed class, and hence satisfies the exact capacity bound \(a+b-1\le u_W\).

It follows that a pure \(W\) parity class using at most two residues modulo \(4\) sends no ordered \(W\)-\(W\) pair to a mixed parity class. With one residue, all midpoint parities equal the source parity. With two residues, same-residue pairs again have the source parity. If the cross-residue midpoint parity were mixed, the capacity bound would give \(a_W-1\le u_W\), because the two subfibers exhaust this pure class. This is impossible: \(3q-1>2q\) and \(27q-1>9q\). All cross pairs have the same midpoint parity, so the existence of even one such outgoing pair would give this contradiction for their whole sumset.

Now fix \(W\in\lbrace\mathrm H,\mathrm L\rbrace\), and let \(S_W\) consist of its atoms in the \(J\) mixed parity classes. Then \(|S_W|=u_WJ\). Let \(I_W\) count ordered \(W\)-\(W\) pairs whose source parity class is pure and whose midpoint lies in \(S_W\). Let \(O_W\) count ordered \(W\)-\(W\) pairs whose source parity class is mixed and whose midpoint lies outside \(S_W\). The preceding capacity argument and the pure-class cardinality give \(I_W\le a_W^2\beta_W\), while \(O_W\ge0\).

Here the source class of a pair is its common endpoint parity. There are exactly \(u_W^2J\) ordered \(W\)-\(W\) pairs with mixed source class, including diagonals. Their midpoints inside \(S_W\) contribute \(u_W^2J-O_W\) to the row count over \(S_W\). The remaining contribution is \(I_W\). Because full extreme-level rows contain precisely these ordered-pair summands, this proves the exact cut identity

$$
\sum_{x\in S_W}h_x=u_W^2J-O_W+I_W.
\tag{6}
$$

Define \(D_W=\sum_{x\in S_W}(h_x-a_W)\). Subtracting \(a_Wu_WJ\) from (6) and using the bounds on \(I_W,O_W\) yields

$$
D_W=I_W-O_W-u_W(a_W-u_W)J
\le a_W^2\beta_W-u_W(a_W-u_W)J.
\tag{7}
$$

By (4), \(\Psi_x=(h_x-a_W)^2/a_W^3\) on \(W\). Cauchy--Schwarz on the nonempty set \(S_W\) therefore gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{x\in S_W}\Psi_x
&\ge\frac{D_W^2}{a_W^3u_WJ}\\
&\ge
\frac{\bigl(u_W(a_W-u_W)J-a_W^2\beta_W\bigr)_+^2}
{a_W^3u_WJ}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}
$$

For the second line, if the positive part is nonzero, (7) makes \(D_W\) negative with at least the displayed magnitude; if it is zero, the bound is nonnegativity. Substitution from (5) gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{x\in S_{\mathrm H}}\Psi_x
&\ge\frac{\bigl(q^2(2J-9\beta_{\mathrm H})\bigr)_+^2}
{54q^4J}
=\frac{(2J-9\beta_{\mathrm H})_+^2}{54J},\\
\sum_{x\in S_{\mathrm L}}\Psi_x
&\ge\frac{\bigl(81q^2(2J-9\beta_{\mathrm L})\bigr)_+^2}
{177147q^4J}
=\frac{(2J-9\beta_{\mathrm L})_+^2}{27J}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{9}
$$

The two center sets are disjoint, so adding (9) proves (1). Its two terms separately give the energy assertions in (2) and the inequalities (3). Dividing (3) by \(J\) proves the stated asymptotic branching requirement. This argument uses actual midpoint sets and exact ordered-pair accounting, rather than assigning row multipliers or counting boundary tails.

For completeness, we verify the full-row price consequence with its original normalizer. As in e7a5a5229669c789 and 3c2a0244e1cbb074, the midpoint-product assumption gives \(H_p(x)=h_xp_x\), and \(\kappa_x\) is uniform on \(R_x\). Sending each ordered same-parity pair to its midpoint and using the common parity-class probability \(1/K\) gives

$$
\sum_{x\in A}h_xp_x^2
=\sum_{\eta}\left(\sum_{x\in A\cap(\eta+2\mathbb Z^n)}p_x\right)^2
=\frac1K.
$$

Consequently, expansion yields

$$
\mathcal V_{\mathcal J}
=\sum_xp_x(Kh_xp_x-1)^2
=K^2b(p)-1
=A_{\mathcal J}-1\ge0.
\tag{10}
$$

Let \(T=\log3\). The only pairs with nonzero score are the \(18q^2J\) unordered \(\mathrm H\)-\(\mathrm L\) pairs within mixed parity classes. Their midpoints have level \(\mathrm B\), and their squared scores equal \(T^2\). For a \(\mathrm B\) center \(x\), let \(r_x\) count these unordered pairs with midpoint \(x\). Distinct reflected pairs have disjoint endpoints, so \(2r_x\le h_x-1\). Uniformity of the row law, counting both orientations, gives

$$
A_{\mathcal J}\nu
=\frac1K\sum_{x\in\mathrm B}2h_xt_{\mathrm B}^3r_xT^2.
\tag{11}
$$

At centers with \(h_xt_{\mathrm B}\le2\), the coefficient of one such pair in the sum before division by \(K\) is at most \(4t_{\mathrm B}^2T^2=4T^2/(81q^2)\). Their total is at most \(8T^2J/9\). At any remaining center, put \(v=h_xt_{\mathrm B}>2\). Its whole contribution is bounded by

$$
2h_xt_{\mathrm B}^3r_xT^2
\le T^2h_x(h_x-1)t_{\mathrm B}^3
\le T^2t_{\mathrm B}v^2
\le4T^2t_{\mathrm B}(v-1)^2
=4T^2\Psi_x.
$$

Each such center is charged once. Hence

$$
A_{\mathcal J}\nu
\le4T^2\mathcal V_{\mathcal J}
+\frac89T^2\frac JK.
\tag{12}
$$

If \(\beta_{\mathrm H}\le J/9\), the bound \(E\ge J/54\) implies \(J/K\le54\mathcal V_{\mathcal J}\), so (12) is at most \(52T^2\mathcal V_{\mathcal J}\). If \(\beta_{\mathrm L}\le J/9\), use \(E\ge J/27\) to obtain \(28T^2\mathcal V_{\mathcal J}\). Finally, for \(A_{\mathcal J}\ge1\), (10) and \((A_{\mathcal J}-1)/A_{\mathcal J}\le\log A_{\mathcal J}\) prove the two price assertions in (2).
statement:
Let \(r\ge2\) be an integer, and set \(q=2^{2r}-1\), \(J=2^r\), \(n=2r+3\), and \(K=2^n=8(q+1)\). Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\) be finite. Give every \(x\in A\) a raw weight \(w_x\in\lbrace9,3,1\rbrace\), and denote the corresponding levels by \(\mathrm H,\mathrm B,\mathrm L\). Suppose every two distinct coordinatewise same-parity atoms \(u,v\in A\) satisfy

$$
\frac{u+v}{2}\in A,
\qquad
w_{(u+v)/2}^{\,2}=w_uw_v.
$$

Require exactly \(q-J\) pure \(\mathrm H\) parity classes with \(3q\) atoms each, \(4q+4\) pure \(\mathrm B\) parity classes with \(9q\) atoms each, \(3q+4\) pure \(\mathrm L\) parity classes with \(27q\) atoms each, and \(J\) mixed parity classes containing \(2q\) atoms of \(\mathrm H\) and \(9q\) atoms of \(\mathrm L\) each. Thus all \(K\) parity classes are occupied.

Use the original normalization and the full-row notation of e7a5a5229669c789 and 3c2a0244e1cbb074:

$$
\begin{aligned}
Z&=\sum_{x\in A}w_x,& p_x&=w_x/Z,& t_x&=Kp_x,\\
R_x&=\lbrace y\in A:2x-y\in A\rbrace,& h_x&=|R_x|,&
\Psi_x&=t_x(h_xt_x-1)^2,\\
H_p(x)&=\sum_{y\in R_x}\sqrt{p_yp_{2x-y}},&
b(p)&=\sum_{x\in A}p_xH_p(x)^2,&
A_{\mathcal J}&=K^2b(p),\\
\kappa_x(y)&=\frac{\sqrt{p_yp_{2x-y}}}{H_p(x)},&
Y_x(y)&=\frac12\log\frac{p_y}{p_{2x-y}},&
\nu&=\frac1{b(p)}\sum_{x\in A}p_xH_p(x)^2
\sum_{y\in R_x}\kappa_x(y)Y_x(y)^2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Write \(E=\sum_{x\in A}\Psi_x\), so \(\mathcal V_{\mathcal J}=E/K\). For \(W\in\lbrace\mathrm H,\mathrm L\rbrace\), let \(\beta_W\) be the number of pure \(W\) parity classes whose atoms occupy at least three distinct coordinatewise residue classes modulo \(4\). With \(s_+=\max\lbrace s,0\rbrace\), every actual realization satisfies

$$
E\ge
\frac{(2J-9\beta_{\mathrm H})_+^2}{54J}
+\frac{(2J-9\beta_{\mathrm L})_+^2}{27J}.
\tag{1}
$$

In particular,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\beta_{\mathrm H}\le J/9
&\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
E\ge J/54,
\qquad
\nu\le52(\log3)^2\log A_{\mathcal J},\\
\beta_{\mathrm L}\le J/9
&\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
E\ge J/27,
\qquad
\nu\le28(\log3)^2\log A_{\mathcal J}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
$$

For arbitrary realizations, the explicit residual requirements are

$$
\beta_{\mathrm H}\ge\frac{2J-\sqrt{54JE}}9,
\qquad
\beta_{\mathrm L}\ge\frac{2J-\sqrt{27JE}}9.
\tag{3}
$$

Consequently, along any sequence of actual realizations with \(r\to\infty\) and \(E/J\to0\), both extreme levels must have at least \(\bigl(2/9-o(1)\bigr)J\) pure parity classes occupying three or more residues modulo \(4\). The constants in (1) and (2) are independent of \(r\), \(q\), and \(J\).
